messages.author: 47597751d567aea1
messages.subject: Re: What does "act" mean when printing summary of a MLP model?
parts:
Hi,

that's the current activation of a unit. This changes with every instance, so it is not too meaningful. What RSNNS shows here are (presumably) the activations of the last instance it has classified. So if you ran it on a test set, the last instance of that test set. Again, as said before, not something that is too useful unless you run the network with a particular instance and want to know what is going on in the network for this instance.

Regards,
Christoph

messages.author: 6b266fd0be5dfe86
messages.subject: RE: What does "act" mean when printing summary of a MLP model?
parts:
Thanks a lot Chris! One more question on the summary.

I understand that for neurons in the hidden layers, they come with biases. However, why there are biases for inputs?

Sincerely,
Johnnie Chen

-----Original Message-----
From: Christoph Bergmeir <christoph...@gmail.com>
Sent: Wednesday, March, 17, 2021 6:16 AM
To: Chen, Johnnie (GZ/RC) <johnni...@kpmg.com>; rs...@googlegroups.com
Subject: Re: What does "act" mean when printing summary of a MLP model?

Hi,

that's the current activation of a unit. This changes with every instance, so it is not too meaningful. What RSNNS shows here are (presumably) the activations of the last instance it has classified. So if you ran it on a test set, the last instance of that test set. Again, as said before, not something that is too useful unless you run the network with a particular instance and want to know what is going on in the network for this instance.

Regards,
Christoph

messages.subject: Re: What does "act" mean when printing summary of a MLP model?
parts:
Hi,

I guess that's just the way SNNS implements this. The input layer has "Act_Identity", which is mapped to "Act_Linear", which has a bias term.

Regards,
Christoph
